common_name: Windham Winter Pea (Dwarf Tannin-Free Cold-Hardy Forage Pea)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast inoculated seed 4-8 weeks before the first hard freeze so plants form a strong crown before winter; Windham's dwarf, upright habit stands better than sprawling Austrian-type peas.

directions: Windham is a white-flowered, tannin-free winter field pea bred for improved cold survival compared with older Austrian winter pea types. Its dwarf, upright canopy stands better than sprawling vine-type peas, and its sweeter, low-tannin foliage is more palatable to grazing livestock and wildlife. Drill seed about 1 inch deep into a firm fall seedbed with fresh inoculant, since like all field peas it needs good rhizobia contact to fix nitrogen effectively. Terminate by mowing, rolling, or incorporation in spring before pod set to capture the fixed nitrogen for a following crop.
sources: Montana State University Foundation Seed Program
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Materials Program

common_name: Survivor Austrian Winter Pea (Small-Leaved Extra-Hardy Forage Pea)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast inoculated seed several weeks before the first hard freeze; Survivor's smaller leaflets and compact growth reduce winter injury where standard Austrian winter pea sometimes fails.

directions: Survivor is a purple-flowered Austrian winter pea selection bred for enhanced cold tolerance, with smaller leaves that reduce winter desiccation and freeze damage relative to older winter pea strains. It is commonly grown alongside cultivars like Whistler and Windham as an option for growers at the colder edge of the winter-pea range. As a viney, nitrogen-fixing legume it benefits from being seeded with a cereal grain such as rye or oats, which gives the tendrils structure to climb while the pea fixes nitrogen for both species. Mow, roll, or till the stand in spring near flowering for the greatest nitrogen contribution ahead of a following crop.

common_name: Frostmaster Winter Pea (Low-Tannin Sweet Forage Pea)

planting.note: Sow in fall, or in early spring in colder regions in place of fall seeding; Frostmaster tolerates a wider planting window than most winter peas thanks to its improved cold hardiness.

directions: Frostmaster is a small-seeded, low-tannin winter forage pea selected for sweeter, more palatable foliage than standard Austrian winter pea, along with noticeably better cold tolerance. Its long, leafy vines produce more forage tonnage than many older winter pea types, making it a favorite for wildlife food plots as well as green-manure cover cropping. Broadcast or drill fresh-inoculated seed into a fall seedbed, or plant in early spring in regions too cold for reliable fall establishment. Because the vines sprawl and climb, mixing with a cereal grain like oats or rye gives the planting more structure and reduces lodging.
sources: Oregon State University Extension Seed Certification Service

common_name: DS Admiral Field Pea (Semi-Leafless Yellow Cover Crop and Grain Pea)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring; DS Admiral is a spring-sown, semi-leafless yellow field pea rather than an overwintering type.

directions: DS Admiral is a yellow-cotyledon field pea long used as an industry standard in western Canadian pea trials, valued for standability and powdery mildew resistance. Its semi-leafless habit, where leaflets are replaced by tendrils, lets plants interlock and stay more upright than conventional-leafed peas, easing mechanical harvest or termination. Drill inoculated seed 1-2 inches deep into cool, workable spring soil, since it germinates well in cold ground and tolerates light spring frosts once established. Use it as a quick-cycling spring nitrogen-fixing cover ahead of a summer crop, or let it mature further for dry pea grain.

common_name: Multicut Berseem Clover (High-Biomass Multi-Cut Berseem Clover)

planting.note: Sow from early spring through late summer in irrigated ground; Multicut has less cold tolerance than Bigbee berseem clover, so it performs best grown as a warm-season annual rather than overwintered.

directions: Multicut is a berseem clover selected for exceptionally high dry-matter production and vigorous nitrogen fixation, outyielding the more cold-hardy Bigbee cultivar under irrigation in warm growing regions. It blooms later and holds a longer vegetative period than earlier-maturing berseem strains, which is what allows repeated cutting through a single season. Broadcast seed onto a firm, moist seedbed and irrigate regularly, since it depends on consistent moisture to support multiple cutting cycles rather than surviving on rainfall alone. Mow or graze every few weeks before flowering to maximize regrowth and biomass, then terminate before seed set.

common_name: Passerel Plus Annual Ryegrass (Rust-Resistant Late-Maturing Italian Ryegrass)

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early fall for winter cover and grazing; Passerel Plus is a later-maturing, disease-resistant selection that stays productive further into spring than common annual ryegrass.

directions: Passerel Plus is an Italian ryegrass cultivar bred for resistance to crown and brown rust along with strong late-fall and spring growth, a top performer in Southeastern cover-crop and grazing trials. Its dense, fibrous root system scavenges leftover soil nitrogen effectively and builds soil structure over winter, while its later maturity extends the window of high-quality forage compared with earlier ryegrass types. Drill or broadcast into a prepared or no-till seedbed in early fall, ensuring good seed-to-soil contact for even establishment. Terminate by mowing, grazing down hard, or herbicide before seed set in spring to prevent it persisting as a volunteer.

common_name: Kentucky Pride Crimson Clover (Cold-Hardy Late-Maturing Crimson Clover)

planting.note: Sow in fall for a winter-to-spring cover; Kentucky Pride survives harder winters than most crimson clover cultivars and flowers roughly two weeks later than older strains like Dixie.

directions: Kentucky Pride is a crimson clover selection recognized for unusually strong winter survival and heavier dry-matter production than older cultivars such as Dixie, giving noticeably better weed suppression through the cool season. Its abundant basal leaves and tillers recover well from mowing or grazing, and its later flowering extends the window of active nitrogen fixation and pollinator forage into mid-spring. Broadcast seed onto a fine, firm seedbed in fall and rake lightly, or drill for more even stands on larger plantings. Terminate at early bloom for maximum nitrogen release, or let a portion go to seed for a self-reseeding stand in future years.

scientific_name: Sorghum bicolor × Sorghum bicolor var. sudanense 'Trudan 8'

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past 65F and frost danger has passed; do not sow into cool spring soil.

directions: Trudan 8 is a fine-stemmed, very leafy sorghum-sudangrass hybrid noted for rapid regrowth after mowing or grazing and for suppressing root-knot nematode populations when its residue is worked in as green manure. The nematode-suppressive effect comes mainly from compounds in the leaves, so mowing and incorporating the stand after a frost or drought stress maximizes the benefit ahead of a following vegetable crop. Broadcast or drill seed into warm summer soil, then mow at roughly knee height before seed heads emerge to keep the stand leafy and encourage dense regrowth rather than tall, woody stems. Terminate by mowing and tillage, or winter-kill, several weeks before a fall planting.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — EDIS
